translations.text: Therefore our hearts and bodies must be made ready to fight under the holy obedience of the commandments; and as for what our nature has less possible in us, let us ask the Lord
that he command the help of his grace to be given to us. And if, fleeing the punishments of hell, we wish to come to eternal life,
then while there is still time, and we are in this body, and there is time to fulfil all these things by this life of light,
we must now run and do what will profit us for eternity.
Therefore a school of the Lord's service must be established by us. In establishing it we hope to set down nothing harsh, nothing burdensome.

But if, as the reason of justice dictates, something a little stricter should come about for the correction of vices or the preservation of love, do not at once flee in terror from the way of salvation, which can only be begun with a narrow beginning. But as one progresses in the monastic life and in faith, with the heart enlarged, the way of God's commandments is run with the unspeakable sweetness of love,

so that, never departing from his teaching, persevering in his doctrine in the monastery until death, we may share by patience in the sufferings of Christ, so that we may also deserve to be sharers in his kingdom.
You who choose to put your neck under the gentle yoke of Christ, give your mind sweetly and willingly to the rule, that you may take honey.

Here is all the teaching of the old law and of the new; here is the divine order; here is the purest life. And the consecrated father composed the holy book. And these commandments he gave to be kept by his sons; and the minister of Christ, concealing [the authorship of] the master's work, brought it forth to all.
One reward awaits both, of both, in eternity. Listen, O son, to the commandments of the master!

And incline the ear of your heart, and willingly receive and effectively fulfil the admonition of the honourable father, so that through the labour of obedience you may return to him from whom you had gone away through the sloth of disobedience. To you, therefore, my word is now directed, whoever you are who, renouncing your own wills, take up the strongest and most glorious weapons of obedience to fight for the Lord Christ, the true king. First of all, whatever good thing you begin to do, ask him with most insistent prayer to bring it to completion,
so that he who has already deigned to count us in the number of his sons may not at any time be grieved by our evil deeds.
For at all times we must obey him with the good things he has given us, so that not only may he not, as an angry father, at any time disinherit his sons, but
also that he may not, as a dreaded lord provoked by our evils, hand over to eternal punishment, as the most wicked servants, those who would not follow him to glory. Let us therefore arise

at last, since Scripture rouses us and says: "It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep." And with our eyes opened to the divine light, let us hear with attentive ears what the divine voice, crying out daily, admonishes us, saying: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts." And again: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.
And what does he say?"
Come, sons, listen to me! I will teach you the fear of the Lord.

Run while you have the light of life, so that the darkness of death does not seize you! And the Lord, seeking his workman among the multitude of the people to whom he calls out these things, says again:
"Who is the man who wants life and longs to see good days?" If you hear this and answer, "I!",
God says to you: If you want to have true and eternal life, keep your tongue from evil, and your lips so that they do not speak deceit!
Turn away from evil and do good! Seek peace and pursue it! And when you do these things,

my eyes will always be upon you and my ears open to your prayers, and before you call on me, I say to you: Here I am. What could be sweeter to us than this voice of the Lord inviting us, dearest brothers?
See how the Lord in his loving-kindness shows us the way of life!

So let us gird our loins with faith, or with the keeping of good deeds, and with our feet shod in readiness for the gospel of peace, let us walk in his paths, so that we may be worthy to see him who calls us into his kingdom. If we wish to dwell in the house of that kingdom, we will not reach it unless we run there by good deeds. But let us ask the Lord with the prophet, saying to him:
Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest on your holy mountain?
After this question, brothers, let us hear the Lord answering and showing us the way to that same house, saying:

He who walks without stain and does what is right; who speaks truth in his heart; who has not practised deceit with his tongue; who has done no evil to his neighbour; who has not taken up a reproach against his neighbour;

who, when the accursed devil tries to persuade him of something, has driven him and his persuasion away from the sight of his heart, rejected him and brought him to nothing, and has taken hold of his small thoughts and dashed them against Christ. Those who fear the Lord do not grow proud of their good observance. Instead, they believe that the good that is in them cannot come from themselves but comes from the Lord.
They praise the Lord who works in them, saying with the prophet: Not to us, Lord, but to your name give glory.
In the same way, the apostle did not credit anything to himself from his preaching, saying: By the grace of God I am what I am. And again he himself says: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord.

That is why the Lord also said: Whoever hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house on rock. The floods came, the winds blew, and [?] struck that house.
And it [?] fell, because it was founded on rock.

Having said all this, the Lord waits for us each day to answer these holy admonitions of his with deeds. For this reason the days of this life are lengthened for us as a respite, so that we may make amends for our evils, as the apostle says: Or do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance? For indeed the merciful one says:
"I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back and live."
So, brothers, when we asked the Lord about who shall dwell in his house, we heard the command given to the one who dwells there.
But if we fulfil the duty of the one who dwells there, we shall be heirs of the kingdom of heaven.
Of the kinds of monks. It is known that there are four kinds of monks. The first is that of the cenobites, that is, the monastic kind, fighting under a rule or an abbot (father).
Then the second kind is that of the anchorites, that is, the hermits (forest-dwellers): those who, not in the fresh fervour of a new life,

but through long probation in the monastery, have learned to fight against the devil, already taught by the help of many; and, well taught, they go from the testing among the brothers to the solitary fight of the wilderness. Secure now, without another's help, they are able, with God helping, to fight with their own hand or arm against the vices of the flesh and of the thoughts.

The third kind of monks, and certainly the worst, is that of the sarabaites. They have not been tested by a rule and by the experience of a master, as gold is tested in the furnace, but are softened like the nature of lead. Still serving the world by their works, they are known to lie in their faith to God by their tonsure. They live in twos or threes, or even alone, without a shepherd, enclosed not in the Lord's sheepfolds but in their own. For their law is the pleasure of their desires. Whatever they think or choose,
that they call holy, and what they do not want, that they consider not permitted.

The fourth kind of monks is called that of the wanderers (gyrovagues). All their life long they go through various provinces and are lodged as guests in various cells for three or four days at a time. They are always wandering and never stable, serving their own wills and the unlawful enticements of the gullet, and in all things worse than the sarabaites.

Of the wretched way of life of all these it is better to be silent than to speak. Leaving these aside, then, let us come, with the Lord's help, to set in order the strongest kind, that of the cenobites.
He who is worthy to be over a monastery must always remember what he is called, and fulfil the name of the greater (superior) by his deeds.
For he is believed to act in the place of Christ in the monastery, since he is called by Christ's own name, as the apostle says:

"You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, in which we cry: Abba, Father." And therefore he must not teach, establish, or command anything outside the Lord's precept, far be it from him. Rather, let his command and his teaching be sprinkled into the minds of the disciples like the leaven of divine justice. Let him always be mindful that in the fearful judgment of God there will be an examination of his teaching and of the obedience of his disciples, of both matters.
And let him know that whatever less profit the father of the household can find in the sheep is laid to the fault of the shepherd.
But it is likewise so that, if all diligence has been applied by the shepherd to a restless or disobedient flock, and every care has been applied to their sick deeds,
their shepherd, acquitted in the Lord's judgment, may say to the Lord with the prophet: "I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have spoken your truth and your salvation.
But they, despising me, scorned me." And then at last, for the sheep disobedient to his care, let death itself be the punishment that prevails over them.

Indeed, when anyone receives the name of abbot, he must govern his disciples with a twofold teaching. That is, he should show all good and holy things by deeds more than by words: to disciples who understand he should set out the Lord's commandments in words, but to the hard of heart and the simpler he should show the divine commandments by his deeds.

Indeed, whatever he teaches his disciples is contrary [to God's law], he should show by his deeds is not to be done, so that he himself is not found reprobate after preaching to others, and so that God does not one day say to him as he sins:
"Why do you declare my justice and take my covenant in your mouth?
You indeed have hated discipline and cast my words behind you." And: "You saw the speck in your brother's eye, but in your own you did not see the beam."

He must not favour one person over another in the monastery. He must not love one more than another, unless it is someone he finds better in good deeds or obedience. A freeborn man must not be placed above one who comes to the monastery from servitude, unless there is some other reasonable cause.
But if, with justice dictating, it so

seems right, he may do that concerning the rank of anyone at all; otherwise, indeed, [let them keep] their own places. For whether slave or free, we are all one in Christ [literally "in the holy one"], and under one Lord we bear equally the warfare of service, for with God there is no partiality toward persons.
In this respect alone are we distinguished in his sight: if we are found better than others in good works and humble.
Indeed, let him show equal love to all, and let one discipline be applied to all, according to their deserts.
Indeed, in his teaching he must always keep the apostolic pattern, in which it says: "Reprove, entreat, rebuke!"
That is, mixing one time with another, gentleness with terrors, he should show the sternness of a master and the loving affection of a father.
That is: he must reprove the undisciplined and restless more harshly, but the obedient and gentle
and patient he should entreat to advance to better things. The negligent and contemptuous, we urge, he should rebuke and correct.

And he must not let the sins of wrongdoers go on, but as soon as they begin to arise, he should cut them out by the root as best he can, mindful of the danger of the priest of Shiloh. Honourable and understanding minds he should indeed correct with words at the first or second warning, but the wicked, the hard, the proud or the disobedient he should restrain with whippings or bodily punishment at the very start of the sin,
knowing that it is written:
"The fool is not corrected by words," and again: "Strike your child with the rod, and you will free his soul from death."

He must always remember what he is [the text here is garbled: "kehuckenti"; Latin "meminere", remember], and what he is called, and know that more is demanded of the one to whom more is entrusted. And he should know how difficult and arduous a task he has taken on: to rule souls and to serve the ways of many, one indeed with gentleness, another indeed with rebukes, another with persuasion. And he should so shape and adapt himself to all according to each one's character or understanding,

And may he not only not suffer losses of the flock entrusted to him, but surely rejoice in the increase of the good flock. Above all, may he not, by overlooking or making little of the salvation of the souls entrusted to him, have more concern for transitory, earthly and perishable things, but let him always consider that he has received souls to govern, for which he must also give account. And let him not complain about perhaps lesser possessions.
Let him remember that it is written: "First seek the kingdom of God and his justice,
and all these things shall be added to you." And again: "Nothing is lacking to those who fear him."

And let him know that he who has received souls to govern must prepare himself to give account. And however great the number of brothers he knows he has under his care, let him know without doubt that on the day of judgment he will have to give account for all these same souls, and without doubt his own soul as well. And so, always fearing the coming examination of the shepherd concerning the sheep entrusted to him, while he is careful about the accounts of others, he becomes careful about his own; and while by his admonitions he ministers correction to others, he himself is made corrected of his vices.
On calling the brothers to council.
As often as any of the more important things are to be done in the monastery, let the abbot call together the whole community and say himself what the matter concerns.
And hearing the counsel of the brothers, let him consider it within himself, and do what he judges more useful.

Therefore we have said that all should be called to council, because the Lord often reveals to the younger what is better. Let the brothers give counsel with all humility of subjection, so that they do not presume to defend stubbornly what seems right to them,
but let it rather depend on the abbot's own judgment, so that whatever he judges to be more salutary, all obey him in it.
But just as it befits disciples to obey the master, so it befits him to arrange all things providently and justly.
In all things, then, let all follow the rule as master, and let no one turn away from it in anything.
Let no one in the monastery follow the will of his own heart, nor let anyone presume to contend insolently with his abbot, inside or outside the monastery.
If he does presume, let him be subject to the discipline of the rule.

The abbot himself, however, should do all things with the fear of God and in observance of the rule, knowing that he will without doubt have to give account of all his judgments to God, the most just judge. But if lesser matters are to be done in the monastery, let him use only the counsel of the seniors, as it is written: "Do all things with counsel, and afterwards you will not repent."
First, to love [?]. Then the neighbour as oneself!
Then: do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not covet, do not speak false witness; honour all men! What one does not want done to oneself, let him not do.

To deny oneself to oneself, in order to follow [?]. To chastise the body, not to embrace pleasures, to love fasting, to refresh the poor, to clothe the naked, to visit the sick, to bury the dead, to help in trouble, to console the grieving, to make oneself a stranger to the deeds of the world, nothing [?] love [?]
…to put before. Not to carry out anger, not to keep a time for wrath, not to hold grief in the heart, not to give a false peace, not to forsake love!
Not to swear, lest perhaps he perjure himself! To bring forth truth from the heart and the mouth, not to repay evil for evil, not to do injury, but to bear patiently what is done to him!
To love enemies! Not to curse back those who curse him, but rather to bless them!

To endure persecution for righteousness, not to be proud, not to be given to wine, not to be a glutton, not to be sleepy, not to be slothful, not to be a grumbler or a slanderer, to commit his hope to God!
When he sees some good in himself, let him attribute it to God, not to himself! But let him know that evil is always done by himself, and let him count it to himself!
To fear the day of judgment, to dread hell,

to long for eternal life with all spiritual desire, to keep death before his eyes daily as something to be feared, to guard the actions of his life at every hour, to know without doubt that God sees him in every place, to dash the evil thoughts that come into his heart against Christ at once and to reveal them to a spiritual elder, to keep his mouth from evil or perverse speech, not to love much talking, not to speak idle words or words fit for laughter, not to love much or boisterous laughter, to listen gladly to holy readings, to devote himself often to prayer, to confess daily to God in prayer, with tears or sighing, his past evils, to amend those same evils from then on, not to fulfil the desires of the flesh, to hate his own will, to obey the commands

in all things, even if he should act otherwise, which God forbid, mindful of the Lord's command: What they say, do; but what they do, choose not to do! Not to be called holy before he is, but first to be so, so that it may more truly be said!
To fulfil God's commands daily in deeds, to love chastity, to hate no one, not to have jealousy and envy, not to love strife, to flee self-exaltation, to honour elders,
to love the younger, in the love of Christ to pray for enemies, to return to peace with one who is at odds with him before the sun sets, and never to despair of God's mercy!

Behold, these are the teachings of the spiritual art. When they have been fulfilled by us unceasingly day and night and handed back on the day of judgment, the reward will be repaid to us by the Lord that he himself promised:
"What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him."
Now the workshops where we diligently work all these things are the enclosures of the monastery and stability in the community.

Of obedience. The first step of humility is obedience without delay. This befits those who regard nothing as dearer to them than Christ, because of the holy service which they have professed, or because of fear of hell or the glory of eternal life.
As soon as anything has been commanded by a superior, as if it were commanded by God, they do not know how to allow delay in doing it. Of them the Lord says: At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me.
Again he says to the teachers:
"He who hears you hears me." Truly, such as these at once leave what is theirs, abandoning their own will, at once with occupied hands

leave unfinished what they were doing, and with the near foot of obedience they follow the voice of the one commanding with deeds. And so, as if in a single moment, the master's command once spoken and the disciple's finished work are both carried out together quickly, in the swiftness of the fear of God,
by those who are pressed by the love of going to eternal life. Therefore they seize the narrow way, of which the Lord says:

"Narrow is the way that leads to life." So, not living by their own judgment, nor obeying their desires and wills, but walking by another's judgment and command, living in community, they desire [?] to be over them.

Without doubt such as these imitate the Lord's saying, in which he says: "I came not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me." But this same obedience is acceptable to God and sweet to men only

if what is commanded is done not hesitantly, not lukewarmly, not slowly, nor with murmuring or with the answer of one who is unwilling, because obedience given to superiors is given to God. For he himself said: "He who hears you hears me."

And it ought to be given by disciples with a good heart, for [?] loves a cheerful giver. For if the disciple obeys with an ill heart, and murmurs not only with his mouth but also in his heart, then even if he fulfils the command, it is no longer acceptable to God,
who sees his heart murmuring. For such a deed no grace follows; rather he incurs the punishment of murmurers, unless he makes amends with due satisfaction.
Let us do what the prophet said: "I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue.
I set a guard on my mouth. I was struck dumb and humbled, and I kept silent even from good things."

Here the prophet shows that if we should sometimes keep silent even from good speech for the sake of silence, how much more should we refrain from evil words because of the punishment of sin. Therefore, even though perfect disciples are allowed to speak about good, holy and edifying things, permission to speak is granted only rarely, because of the seriousness of silence. For it is written: "In much speaking you will not escape sin." And in another place it says: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue."
Truly, it is fitting for the master to speak and teach; it is proper for the disciple to keep silent and listen.
Therefore, if anything has to be asked of superiors, let it be asked with the utmost reverence, so that one does not seem to speak more than is needful.
But jests, idle words, and words that stir up laughter we condemn everywhere and shut out forever. And we do not allow a disciple to open his mouth for such talk.

Holy Scripture cries out to us, saying: "Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted." When it says this, it shows us that every exaltation is a kind of pride. The prophet shows that he guards himself against this when he says:
"Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up, nor have I walked in great things, nor in wonders beyond me.
"If not humbly, but I exalted my soul, as a weaned child is upon its mother, so repay it upon my soul!"

Therefore, if we wish to reach the summit of the highest humility, and wish to come quickly to that heavenly exaltation to which one rises through the humility of the present life, then by our rising deeds that very ladder must be set up which appeared in a dream, on which descending
and ascending ones were shown to him.
Without doubt we understand that descent and ascent to mean nothing other than descending by exaltation and ascending by humility.
Truly, that upright ladder is our life in the world, which, once the heart is humbled, is raised up by the Lord to heaven.

Truly, we say that the sides of that ladder are our body and soul. Into these sides the divine calling has set various steps of humility or discipline, for those who climb. So the first step of humility is this: that a man always sets the fear of God before his eyes and flees forgetfulness entirely, and always remembers everything that God has commanded. He should always turn over in his mind how hell burns for their sins those who despise God, and likewise the eternal life that is prepared for those who fear God.

And he should guard himself at every hour from sin and vice, that is, sins of the thoughts, the tongue, the eyes, the hands, the feet, or his own will, and he should also hasten to cut off the desires of the flesh. Let a man consider that he is always seen from heaven by God at every hour, and that his deeds are seen in every place by the sight of the Godhead, and are by [?]
reported at every hour. The prophet shows us this when he shows that God is always present in our thoughts, saying:

"God searches the hearts and the reins." And again: "The Lord knows the thoughts of men." And again he says: "You have understood my thoughts from afar." And: "The thought of man shall confess to you." Truly, so that he may be watchful about his perverse thoughts, let the profitable one always say
in his heart:
"Then I shall be spotless before him, if I keep myself from my iniquity."
Truly, we are forbidden to do our own will, since Scripture says to us: "And turn away from your own wills."
Again, we ask God in prayer that his will be done in us. Truly, then, we are rightly taught not to do our own will, when we beware of what Holy Scripture says:
"There are ways which are thought right by men, whose end sinks down to the depth of hell."

And again, when we beware of what is said of the negligent: "They are corrupted and have become abominable in their wills." Truly, let us believe that God is always present to us in the desires of the flesh, since the prophet says to the Lord: "Before you is all my desire." Therefore we must beware of evil desire,
because death is placed beside the entrance of pleasure.

Hence Scripture commands, saying: "Do not go after your desires." Truly, if the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil, and he always looks down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God,
and if our works are reported daily, by day and by night, to the Lord our maker by the angels assigned to us, then one must truly be on guard at every hour,

as the prophet says in the psalm, lest God see us at any hour turning aside into evil and become useless. And though he spares us in this time, because he is merciful and waits for us daily to be turned toward the better, let him not say to us in the time to come: "These things you did, and I kept silent."
The second step of humility is if someone, not loving his own will, takes no delight in fulfilling his desires, but imitates in deeds that voice
of the one [?] saying: "I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me." Again Scripture says: "Self-will has punishment, and necessity brings forth a crown."
The third step of humility is that someone, for the love of God, submits himself in all obedience to a superior, imitating the Lord, of whom the Apostle says: "He became obedient even unto death."

The fourth, if in this same obedience, when things are hard and contrary, or even when any injuries whatever are inflicted, he embraces [?] with a silent mind, and enduring does not grow weary or go away, as Scripture says: "He who perseveres

to the end, he shall be saved." Likewise: "Let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord." And showing that the faithful man must endure all things for the Lord, even contrary things, it says in the person of those who suffer: "For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for the slaughter." [?]
And secure in the hope of the divine reward, they follow after, rejoicing and saying: "But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us."
Likewise in another place: "You have tested us; you have tried us with fire, as silver is tried with fire.
You led us into the snare; you laid hardship upon our back."
And to show that we must be under a superior, it follows, saying: "You set men over our heads." And also the command

[?] in adversities and injuries: those who are struck on the cheek offer the other as well; to the one who takes away the tunic they also give up the cloak; when forced to go one mile, they go two; and with Paul the Apostle they endure false brothers, and endure persecution, and bless those who speak evil of them.
The fifth, if he does not conceal, through humble confession, all the evil thoughts that come into his heart, or the evils he has done in secret,
from his own [?], Scripture urging us concerning this matter and saying: "Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him."
Again: "Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever." Again: "I made my transgression known to you; [?] I covered my injustices.
I said: I will declare my injustice against myself, Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin." The sixth, if a monk, content with every meanness and utmost lowliness,

in all the things that are laid on him, he judges himself a bad and unworthy workman, saying to himself with the prophet: "I have been brought to nothing and I did not know it; I have become like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you."

The seventh, if he declares himself lower and baser than all, not only with his tongue but also believes it with the innermost love of his heart, humbling himself and saying with the prophet: "But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and an outcast of the people"; "exalted, humbled, confounded"; and again: "It is good for me
that you have humbled me, so that I may learn your commandments!"

The eighth, if he does nothing except what the common rule of the monastery or the examples of the elders urge. If he keeps his tongue from speaking and, keeping silence, does not speak until he is asked, as Scripture says, that "in much speaking sin is not escaped" and that "a talkative man is not set straight upon the earth."
The tenth, if he is not easy and quick to laughter, for it is written: "The fool raises his voice in laughter." He speaks gently,
without laughter, humbly, with seriousness; he speaks few and reasonable words, and is not loud of voice, as it is written:
"The wise man is known by few words." The twelfth, if he always shows humility not only in his heart but also in his very body to those who see him, that is, in work,
in the garden,

on the road, in the field, or wherever he is, sitting, walking or standing, with his head always bowed and his eyes fixed on the ground; at every hour he considers himself guilty of his sins and thinks himself already brought before the dreadful judgment, always saying in his heart what the publican of the Gospel said with his eyes fixed on the ground: "I, a sinner, am not worthy to lift my eyes to heaven"; and again with the prophet: "I am bowed down and humbled on every side."
"So when all these steps of humility have been climbed, he will soon arrive at that love of God

which, being perfect, casts out fear. Through it he will begin to keep without any effort, as if naturally and from habit, everything he used to observe not without fear. He will keep it no longer out of fear of hell but out of love, and out of that same good habit, [and] the delight of the virtues. The Lord will deign to show this by the Holy Spirit in his workman, now cleansed of vices and sins.

In wintertime, according to the consideration of reason, one is to rise at the eighth hour of the night, so that one rests a little beyond midnight and rises likewise having digested. What remains after the vigils is to be used by those brothers who need some part of the psalter
or of the readings, for study. From
however,

to the time mentioned above, let the time be arranged so that the vigils are done with a very short interval, in which the brothers go out for the needs of nature. Immediately afterwards the morning lauds, which are to be done as the light begins, follow.
written above, first the verse; in the second [?] it is to be said: "will proclaim"
To which the third psalm is to be added
After this psalm the ninety-fourth:
with antiphons, or at least to be sung.

After this let six psalms follow. When these have been said and the verse has been said, let [?] bless, and with all sitting on the benches, let three readings be [?] in turn by the brothers from the book on the lectern, between which three
Truly, after the third, let the one who sings say the Glory.

When the singer begins to say it, let all at once rise from their seats, out of honour and reverence for the Holy Trinity. Let books of divine authority be read at the vigils, from the Old Law as well as from the New, and also their expositions, which were made by named teachers and orthodox fathers.
After these three lessons with their responsories, let the other six psalms follow, to be sung.
After these, let the lesson of the Apostle follow, to be recited from memory, and the humble prayer "Lord, have mercy on us." Thus let the vigils of the night be ended.
In all of them, as was said above, let the quantity of psalm-singing be kept, except
that the lessons from the book are not to be read at all, because of the shortness of the nights.

Instead of the three lessons, let one from the Old Law be read from memory, and let a short [?] follow it. Let everything else be completed as was said. That is, never let less than the quantity of twelve psalms be said at vigils, besides the third
and the ninety-fourth psalm.

On the Lord's days let them rise earlier for vigils. At these vigils let the measure be kept, that is, after singing as we set out above [?], with all again seated in proper order on the benches, let four lessons with their responsories be read from the book, as we said above.

Let this order of vigils be kept in the same way at every season, summer and winter alike, on the Lord's day. The exception is if perhaps (God forbid) they rise too late. Then something must be shortened from the lessons or from the responsories.
However, let every care be taken that this does not happen. If it does happen, let the one through whose negligence it came about make worthy amends for it to God in the church.

Certainly, let the morning office or the evening office never pass by unless at the very end, in its order, the Lord's Prayer is said by the superior with everyone listening, because of the thorns of scandal that usually spring up. In this way those who are brought together by the promise of that same prayer, in which they say, "Forgive us, as we also forgive," may cleanse themselves of such a fault.
At the other offices, though, let the last part of the prayer be said, so that everyone answers: "But deliver us from evil."

let him be chosen from the congregation: wise, of mature character, sober, not a great eater, not proud, not turbulent, not hostile-minded, not slow, not wasteful, but fearing God, one who shall be like a father to the whole congregation.
Let him take care of everything; let him do nothing without the abbot's command; let him keep to what is commanded; let him not sadden [the brothers].

If anyone asks him for something unreasonable at some time, let him not sadden him by spurning him, but reasonably and with humility refuse the one who asks wrongly. Let him guard his own soul, always mindful of that apostolic saying, that "he who ministers well acquires a good standing for himself."
Let him take care of the sick, of children, of guests and of the poor with all solicitude, knowing without doubt that he will have to render account for all these on the day of judgement.
Let him regard all the vessels and all the property as though they were the consecrated vessels of the altar.

Let him treat nothing as something to neglect, and let him not be wasteful or an uprooter of the property of the monastery, but let him do everything in measure and according to the command of the abbot.
Let him have humility before all things, and to one to whom there is nothing to give, let a good word of answer be offered, as it is written: "A good word is above the best gift."

[Those to whom God gives] the endurance of abstinence [should know] they will have their own reward. [If] necessity [or work or] the heat of summer demands more, let it stand in the prior's own judgment, [taking care] that neither satiety nor drunkenness creeps in [and] hinders [?].
Although we read that [wine is not for monks at all], that cannot be urged [on monks] in our times. Yet let us at least agree to this: [that we drink] not to satiety but more sparingly,

[for wine] makes even the wise fall away. [Where] necessity demands that the measure written above [cannot be found], but much less or none at all, [let those who live there bless God] [?], and let the monks be without murmuring.

From holy Easter [to Pentecost] let them eat [at midday] and take supper at night. From Pentecost, [throughout] the summer, if field work or excessive summer heat does not trouble [them], [let them fast] on the fourth and sixth days [Wednesdays and Fridays],
[and] on other days [let them] dine. If they have their own [work] in the fields, or the heat is too great, that dinner [time] is to be kept up, [at the abbot's] foresight.

Let him temper and arrange [everything] so that souls may be saved and [the brothers] do what they do without murmuring. [From mid-September] up to the beginning of the fast, [let them eat at the ninth hour]; from [the beginning of] the fast [until Easter], at evening.
Let that evening [meal] be held so that those eating do not need the light of a lamp, but let everything be finished while there is still daylight. [At every time,] whether supper or dinner,
let it be so arranged that everything is [done] by daylight.
At every time [monks] must strive for silence, most of all at the night hours. At every time, whether [of fasting] or of dinner,

At the time of the divine office, as soon as the signal has been heard, let them leave everything that is in their hands and run with the greatest haste, yet with gravity, so that foolery does not find tinder. Idleness is the enemy of the soul; [therefore the brothers] must be occupied at fixed times [in manual labour, and at fixed times in reading]. Likewise, [until the time when] they do the sixth [hour], let them be free [for reading]. Let [None] be done earlier, at the middle of the eighth hour, [and let them again do the work that is to be done] until evening. [If necessity or] poverty requires that they be occupied with gathering the crops [themselves], let them not be saddened.

Yet let everything be done in moderation, for the sake of the faint-hearted. [From the Kalends of October] until the beginning of the fast [Lent], let them be free [for reading] until the second hour is complete; at the second hour let Terce be done.

At the first signal for the ninth hour, let each one leave off his work and be ready when the second signal sounds. As soon as the signal is heard, let everyone leave whatever [they have in hand] and run with the greatest haste.

Of clerics
…with the same desire to be joined [to the monastery], let them be placed in the middle rank; the same [let them] promise the keeping [of the rule] and their own stability.
A pilgrim from distant lands, to dwell as a guest … [if he] does not disturb [the monastery] by his excess, [but is] simply [content], let him be received for as long a time as he desires.
If indeed he reasonably, with the humility of love, criticizes or points out anything, let [the abbot] consider prudently whether [the Lord] directed him for this very thing.

Afterwards, [if he wishes] to confirm his stability, let such [a wish] not be refused, above all because in the time of hospitality [his life] could be made known. [But if he was] found excessive or full of vices…

…[in the time of] hospitality, to be joined to the body [of the monastery]; but rather let him be told honourably to depart, lest by his wretchedness [others] also be corrupted. [If he is not such a one as] deserves to be cast out, [if] he asks [?]…
…to be joined, let him be persuaded to stay, so that by his example others may be taught; [for in every place] one Lord is served, for one King one does battle. [If the abbot] has perceived such…

…let it be permitted [to place him] in a somewhat higher place [?]. [Also] from the above-written grades of priests [the abbot may establish them] to stand in a higher place than the one in which they entered…

…[if he] perceives such [to be their] life. Let [the abbot] beware ever [to receive a monk] from [another] known [monastery] to dwell, [without?] the consent [of his abbot] or a letter of commendation.

The younger [let them honour] their elders.
